Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Goal 2 Gameplay 3 Victory points 4 End of Game Goal To win, prove you’re the most experienced traveler by moving around the map and scoring Victory Points (VP). Gameplay At the start of the game, two random Journey effects are selected. These stay in place for the whole game. Players take turns. On your turn, do the following in order: Optionally Fly : If you are at an Airport you may move to a different one. Move : Discard one or more Trek cards to move a number of steps equal to the numbers on them. (Suits are ignored.) You must move if you can. If you land on a cube, pick it up and put it in your suitcase. Action : Either Draw Two (draw two cards from the row and/or top of the draw deck), Take a Tour (claim a Destination card by discarding Trek cards that match its color requirements) or Journey (discard two cards of the same colour to trigger either Journey bonus effect) Victory points A golden compass indicates Victory Points. Collect these wherever you can. Find them on: Destination cards : Visit places shown on Destination cards and then “Take a Tour” to experience their wonder and history. Destination cards will earn you a lot of Victory Points. Victory Point tokens : Touring some Destinations will earn you an additional 3 or 5 Victory Point token. Some Journey cards also give Victory Point tokens. Your Suitcase : As you travel around the map you will collect Souvenir cubes, which are kept in your suitcase. Collecting sets of different color Souvenirs will earn you Victory Points. Most Souvenirs tiles : Collecting enough Souvenir cubes of any one color can earn you the matching Most Souvenirs tile, which is worth Victory Points. Region Bonus tokens : Collecting the last Souvenir from a region lets you collect a Region Bonus token. Each Region Bonus token you collect is kept secret and is worth between 2 and 6 Victory Points. End of Game The game ends when 5 of the 6 Region Bonus tokens have been claimed, or when a player Tours their fifth Destination card. In either case, the player who triggered the end finishes their turn and the game ends. We designed Trekking the World for gamers and non-gamers to play together. The goal was to make a game inviting for non-gamers, but with a little subtlety under the hood for gamers.

Gleaming monuments and sunrise vistas await your arrival as you traverse the globe to experience its many wonders. Will you explore ancient ruins deep in the jungle, or go wild on a savanna safari? Build your bucket list of destinations and take a whirlwind tour to visit them all - but hurry, your fellow travelers might just beat you there!

In Trekking the World 2-5 players compete to be the ultimate globe trotter by racing to visit world-renowned locations and collect rare souvenirs along the way. The game spotlights 48 real-world destinations, each beautifully illustrated and accompanied with educational passages to inspire your next getaway.

—description from the publisher
community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Too light for gamers but this would be fine as a gateway/kids game and offers a little geographical knowledge.  There is a little planning of future turns required to be efficient but most decisions are obvious. + Cards are dual use, for moving and for collecting tours (points) + Theme supports the game concept – Luck in card draw

[Rating: 1/10] If you're going to engage in a boring "travel the world" game whose rate of success is aggravatingly luck-based, just play TICKET TO RIDE.

[Rating: 2/10] Traded for Marvel Champions w/ Gugong  Get and play Ticket to ride instead. This is not good.

[Rating: 3/10] Game looks great, but I was disappointed in the gameplay. Have played at both 2p and 4p. It appears to be about completing trips at landmark sites, but the game timer and points seem far more based on just moving around and collecting sets of cubes.

[Rating: 3/10] Update: How is it 2020 and people are still releasing games that end immediately when a trigger is hit, without giving players equal turns? Especially in a game like this where 1st player is already has a lead on everyone else for being able to complete contracts (or whatever they're called). It really boggles my mind. Especially in a game where players typically make no points in a turn, but the ability to complete the contract they're working on is critical. A house rule to give all players an equal number of turns is the MINIMUM house rule required here. Doesn't matter to me, though. I won'

[Rating: 3/10] Easy to teach, very simple rules. Nothing newReally light, the decisions are either obvious or random. It's variable, even when this game didn't really need it.  It's waaaay too long and repetitive and this is the final blow to this game. I see that this third version of the game features improvements, but there's barely enough for just one game. There are much better ones thatt deserve second chances.

[Rating: 3/10] The game looks good, but the end game is unfair, and some journey cards are downright broken (catch me if you can)... For new players might be good, but for strategic mind players is just bad...

[Rating: 3/10] (Played on BGA)  Maybe the tactility of the physical game gives it some extra points with people, but this game is pretty terrible for anyone who's played games for a short while.  A gateway game? Perhaps?

[Rating: 3/10] Trekking the national parks is way better  This game its so hard to get stuff done without a ton of luck or nobody screwing you  Its terrible

[Rating: 3/10] Wow is this game boring! Preferred National Parks, but not sure why. Luck in the movement cards, luck in the destination cards, luck in being where you need to be at the right time. It's fine as a kid friendly family game, but I never want to play again. Why play this over Ticket to Ride?

[Rating: 4/10] A rather bland card-movement gateway game, spending cards to move around a world map and/or achieve goals in specific locations. There are some admittedly neat extra mechanics stacked on top to keep older players interested, but it doesn't really add up to much.

[Rating: 4/10] Immensely similar to its prequel [thing=154428][/thing].  Majorities are much more important here with no second place and obligatory movement harshly cutting into the card economy.  Simple dual-use trek card drafting drives set collection to complete tours and movement used to collect souvenirs for majority scoring.  Players aim to optimize their movement to both collect a souvenir while also getting in position to visit a high-value Touring spot. Because one has to move every turn, players can theoretically jostle for position, but colliding with each other is so circumstantial as to rarely
